questions.question: A tibble `emis` (the main data, one row per country and year) is to be combined with a tibble `gdp` that lacks some country-years and has a few extra ones. Every row of `emis` must be kept, with gross domestic product (GDP) added where it exists. Which call does this?
For two tibbles `a` and `b` with a common key column `id`, which rows does `a %>% right_join(b, by = "id")` always keep?
options: every row of `a`, the table the pipe starts from
only the rows whose `id` occurs in both tables
every row of `a` and every row of `b`
every row of `b`, the table inside the call

questions.question: Tibble `x` has the columns `id`, `year` and `sales`; tibble `y` has `id`, `year` and `price`. Which columns does `x %>% left_join(y)` use as keys when `by` is left out?
options: `id` and `year`, the column names both tables share
only `id`, the first column of each of the two tables
none: without `by` the join stops with an error
every column of `x`, so `sales` must also occur in `y`

questions.question: With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3, 4), a = c(5, 6, 7, 8))` and `y <- tibble(id = c(2, 4, 6), b = c(20, 40, 60))`, what does `nrow(inner_join(x, y, by = "id"))` return?
With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3))` and `y <- tibble(id = c(3, 1), b = c(30, 10))`, what does `x %>% left_join(y, by = "id") %>% pull(b)` return?
With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3), a = c(5, 6, 7))` and `y <- tibble(id = c(2, 3, 5), b = c(1, 1, 1))`, what does `x %>% full_join(y, by = "id") %>% pull(id)` return?
With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3, 4), a = c(5, 6, 7, 8))` and `y <- tibble(id = c(2, 4, 9), b = c(20, 40, 90))`, what does `x %>% right_join(y, by = "id") %>% pull(a)` return?

With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(country = c("NL", "NL", "BE", "BE"), year = c(2020, 2021, 2020, 2021))` and `y <- tibble(country = c("NL", "BE", "BE", "DE"), year = c(2021, 2020, 2022, 2020))`, what does `nrow(inner_join(x, y, by = c("country", "year")))` return?
options: an error, because `by` may name only one column

questions.question: With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(country = c("NL", "BE", "DE"))` and `y <- tibble(country = c("nl", "BE", "DE"), gdp = c(900, 525, 3890))`, what does `x %>% left_join(y, by = "country") %>% pull(gdp)` return?
With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(id = c(1, 2), value = c(5, 6))` and `y <- tibble(id = c(1, 2), value = c(7, 8))`, what does `names(left_join(x, y, by = "id"))` return?
For two tibbles `x` and `y` with a key column `id`, which call keeps the same rows as `x %>% right_join(y, by = "id")`, possibly with the columns in a different order?

Tibble `emis` has one row per country and year with column `co2`, and tibble `gdp` has one row per country and year with column `gdp`; each country appears for several years in both. Which `by` should a join of the two use?
Tibble `x` has 5 rows and tibble `y` has 4 rows, and every `id` occurs at most once in each table. `inner_join(x, y, by = "id")` has 3 rows. How many rows does `full_join(x, y, by = "id")` have?

For tibbles `x` and `y` with a key column `id`, where `y` has a column `b` without missing values, which expression marks exactly the rows of `x` that will have `NA` in `b` after `left_join(x, y, by = "id")`?
With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(id = c(1, 1, 2))` and `y <- tibble(id = c(1, 2), price = c(5, 7))`, what does `x %>% left_join(y, by = "id") %>% pull(price)` return?
options: an error, because the key `id` repeats in `x`

questions.question: With the tidyverse attached, the tibbles `x` and `y` each have 6 rows: the countries NL and BE, each for the years 2019, 2020 and 2021, one row per country and year. How many rows does `inner_join(x, y, by = "country")` return?

Tibble `x` has the columns `id` and `sales`; tibble `y` has `id` and `price`. Which condition guarantees that `x %>% left_join(y, by = "id") %>% filter(!is.na(price))` keeps exactly the rows of `x %>% inner_join(y, by = "id")`?
options: The column `price` in `y` has no missing values.
No condition is needed; the two always agree.
Each `id` occurs at most once in each table.

questions.question: For any two tibbles `x` and `y` joined on a key column `id`, keys may repeat within a table. Which statement about the numbers of rows always holds?
options: `left_join(x, y)` has exactly as many rows as `x`.
`right_join(x, y)` never has more rows than `y`.
`full_join(x, y)` never has more rows than `x` and `y` together.
`inner_join(x, y)` never has more rows than `left_join(x, y)`.

questions.question: With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3, 4))`, `y <- tibble(id = c(2, 3), b = c(20, 30))` and `z <- tibble(id = c(3, 4, 5), d = c(7, 8, 9))`, what does `x %>% left_join(y, by = "id") %>% inner_join(z, by = "id") %>% nrow()` return?
With the tidyverse attached, `x <- tibble(id = c(1, 2, 3))` and `y <- tibble(id = c(1, 1, 2), b = c(4, 5, 6))`, what are `nrow(inner_join(x, y, by = "id"))` and `sum(x[["id"]] %in% y[["id"]])`?
